current_example.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/a2dfb286623876334429ecc58985799281561c48906e5f79a955b7ab007565d4.svg)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

- From the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/4ff8e8fde008e78dd4d285a6d54e9a199a893487b0550b8497912ea477ab6dde.svg) we deduce that $\textrm{Re}(\lambda)={\color{blue}3}$ and $\textrm{Im}(\lambda) = {\color{red}-1}.$ So, our eigenvalue is

$$
\lambda = {\color{blue}3}+({\color{red}-1})\text{i} = 3-\text{i}.
$$

- From the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/70b29070b667a3cd1f1a45b845ef693ce1132843000bab848e21f05f511aac2d.svg) we deduce that our corresponding eigenvector is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14244484/assets/92680ed0c239086ce6e6999c9d8e048aadfd1de5dbef36cf0aaef3235ddf2988.svg)

Finally, the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda,$ and the second eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Therefore, our eigenvalues and eigenvectors are
